newsitem.title: UK: Euro bourses fret over Wall St, elections, EMU.
newsitem.headline: Euro bourses fret over Wall St, elections, EMU.

text.p: European bourses closed lower on Tuesday as worries grew about the health of Wall Street, while London also suffered pre-election jitters and Germany fretted over monetary union.

The dollar slid against the mark, losing about 1.5 pfennigs from Monday's close, after a senior Bundesbanker said European economic and monetary union (EMU) should be delayed if Germany could not meet the entry criteria.

German stocks tumbled 1.78 percent in response but share markets across the continent also worried about the state of the U.S. market, with Wall Street guru Warren Buffett saying most stocks are overvalued.

The mood was further depressed by the ever-present fear that the U.S. central bank would make a pre-emptive strike against inflation by raising interest rates when its Federal Open Market Committee meets on March 25.
Wall Street itself added to the gloom and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 27.19 at 6,928.29 as the European exchanges closed.
European investors also had worries of their own.

London, which shrugged off Prime Minister John Major's announcement of a May 1 parliamentary election on Monday, started worrying about a six-week campaign and the prospect of a change in government. The blue-chip FTSE-100 index closed down 16.5 points at 4,356.8.
The election date came as no surprise to markets, but with the opposition far ahead in opinion polls, traders began to contemplate life under a Labour government.
Financial markets are traditionally hostile to Labour, but leader Tony Blair has dragged the party towards the political centre and made efforts to woo the business community.
"Even though everybody expects Labour to win, the election campaign will still be a factor, it's another reason for people to sit on their hands and stay out of the market," one trader said.
Speculation centres on what tax plans Labour will reveal if it wins. "It is not a happy scenario ... I would not want to be active buyer here," the trader said.
Other European equity markets were likewise weak. In Paris the CAC-40 index closed down 14.43 points or 0.56 percent at 2,573.95 after diving two percent on Monday.
But Germany suffered the most with the DAX closing down 59.8 points at 3,291.19.

Concern is growing that Bonn might fail to cut its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year, a target for EMU membership, forcing a delay in the project's scheduled start in January 1999.

Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher was quoted on Tuesday as doubting that Bonn could meet convergence targets and the start of EMU could have to be delayed. "If Germany can't meet EMU targets the markets are going to fall sharply," one senior trader said.
Frankfurt also buzzed about Hoesch-Krupp's plan to bid for steel giant Thyssen AG . Shares in both were suspended by the German stock exchange.
Thyssen has said it would use "all appropriate measures" to ward off its smaller rival.
On foreign exchange markets, the dollar slid to 1.6757 marks from 1.6901 in European trading late on Monday, and to 122.42 yen from 123.63.
As on the equity markets, Kuehbacher's comments on EMU and U.S. interest rates were major talking points.

"Kuehbacher's comments are surprisingly forthright, but the Buba guys can say what they like -- it's still down to the politicians to make the decision," said Thomas Rayner, economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull.
Investors usually seek refuge in the mark when they worry about EMU. But analysts said expectations of positive German data this week were also helping the mark.

Key German indicators this week, including an Ifo survey and M3 money supply, could offset the possibility of higher U.S. rates after robust American data, including housing starts, were released on Tuesday.

Total housing starts shot up 12.2 percent in February, the strongest growth since March 1994. "The housing numbers were quite strong," said David Bloom, currency strategist at HSBC James Capel. "The market has factored in a good possibility of a Fed rate hike."
Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony to the Joint Economic Committee on Thursday will be watched closely for clues on U.S. monetary policy.

Announcement of a Japanese government scheme to improve land sales helped the yen, along with comments from a Bank of Japan official which dealers interpreted as a check on falling long-term interest rates.
CURRENCIES AT EUROPEAN CLOSE
The dollar was quoted at 1.6757 marks and 122.42 yen, compared with Monday's late European levels of 1.6901 marks and 123.63 yen.
STOCK MARKETS AT CLOSE
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index closed down 16.5 points at 4,356.8.
PARIS - The CAC-40 closed down 14.43 points at 2,573.95.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index closed down 59.80 (1.78 percent) at 3,291.19. In later electronic trading, the IBIS index closed down 47.52 points at 3,289.59.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold closed at $347.05 an ounce after being fixed at $346.30 an ounce in the afternoon and compared with $350.25 at the close on Monday. Silver was at $5.12, compared with $5.23 on Monday.
